items.title: Tilting your phone changes things differently depending on the order
items.claim: Take a book. Rotate 90 degrees about its vertical axis, then 90 degrees about its horizontal axis. Now reset and reverse the order: horizontal first, then vertical. The book ends up in a DIFFERENT orientation. Rotations in 3D do not commute.

options.text: Rotation matrices in 3D are non-commutative — R1 * R2 is not equal to R2 * R1 in general. SO(3) is a non-abelian Lie group, unlike rotations in 2D which DO commute

items.reveal:
Rotations in 2D (the plane): R(theta1) * R(theta2) = R(theta1 + theta2) = R(theta2) * R(theta1). They commute. The group SO(2) is abelian.

Rotations in 3D: not commutative. The group SO(3) is non-abelian. The order in which you apply rotations changes the final orientation.

Experiment: rotate book 90° about vertical (y-axis) — left becomes back. Then rotate 90° about (now front-pointing) x-axis — back becomes bottom. Reset. Now rotate 90° about x first — top becomes back. Then 90° about y — back becomes left. Final orientations differ.

Mathematically: if R_x is rotation about x-axis and R_y about y-axis, R_x R_y is not equal to R_y R_x. The 'commutator' [R_x, R_y] = R_x R_y - R_y R_x is non-zero, representing a small rotation about the third axis.

Consequences:
- Aerospace: gimbal lock — a 3-axis gyroscope can have its three rotation axes align such that one rotational degree of freedom is lost. Famously almost killed Apollo astronauts on Apollo 11.
- Quaternions (Hamilton 1843) parametrise 3D rotations without gimbal lock and are standard in 3D graphics.
- Quantum mechanics: angular momentum operators have the same commutation structure as 3D rotations, leading to quantisation.

In higher dimensions (n > 3), rotation groups SO(n) are also non-commutative.
items.why: Rotation seems like a simple geometric concept. In 3D it's surprisingly subtle — the order matters, and that fact has cost lives, structured quantum mechanics, and shaped every video game engine.

items.title: Cutting an integral into 100 trapezoids beats analytical integration for most real problems
items.claim: Most integrals appearing in physics, engineering or statistics do NOT have closed-form solutions. They're computed numerically. The simplest method (trapezoidal rule) divides the interval into strips and approximates each as a trapezoid.

options.text: Error in the trapezoidal rule is O(1/n^2) where n is the number of strips. Simpson's rule (quadratic interpolation) is O(1/n^4). Gauss-Legendre and adaptive quadrature can achieve essentially machine precision for well-behaved integrands
Always less accurate than analytical answers

items.reveal:
Trapezoidal rule: approximate integral from a to b of f(x) dx by the sum of trapezoidal strips. Error scales as h^2 (where h is the strip width), so halving h quarters the error.

Simpson's rule (uses quadratic fits to triples of points): error scales as h^4. Halving h reduces error by 16x.

For a function smooth enough on [a, b], Simpson's rule with 20 strips can give 6-7 decimal places of accuracy. Gauss-Legendre quadrature with 10 nodes can give 10-15 decimal places.

Many real-world integrals:
- integral of e^(-x^2) dx: no elementary antiderivative. Used everywhere in statistics. Always computed numerically (or via the error function erf).
- integral of sin(x)/x dx: no elementary form. Defined as the sine integral Si(x).
- integral over irregular domains, multidimensional integrals, integrals with singularities — numerical methods are standard.

Monte Carlo integration: for high-dimensional integrals (d > ~4), grid-based methods (Simpson, Gauss) suffer the 'curse of dimensionality' — n grid points per axis means n^d total. Monte Carlo (random sampling) has error O(1/sqrt(N)) independent of dimension; the standard tool for integrals in 10+ dimensions (e.g., statistical mechanics, finance).

More sophisticated: adaptive quadrature (refines where the function is wiggly), Romberg's method, Chebyshev quadrature for analytic functions, sparse grids, quasi-Monte Carlo with low-discrepancy sequences (Sobol, Halton).

The trade-off between numerical and analytical: analytical is exact when available, but unavailable for most functions. Numerical is universally applicable, with accuracy dialed up by computational cost.
items.why: Calculus class focuses on analytical integration. Real applied math is largely numerical — and the numerical methods can be vastly faster and more accurate than the analytical ones for the integrals actually needed.

items.title: Most people earn less than the average wage
items.claim: If you tell people the 'average wage' in their country, most of them are below it. This isn't a fluke — it's a feature of skewed distributions like income, where a few huge values pull the mean up but most observations sit lower.
items.prompt: What's the difference that matters here?

options.text: There is no difference — these terms are interchangeable
Mean (arithmetic average) is pulled by extreme values; median (50th percentile) splits the population in half; for income distributions, the mean is well above the median because of high earners

items.reveal:
Three common 'averages':
- Mean: sum of values divided by count. Sensitive to extreme values.
- Median: the middle value when sorted. Robust to extremes.
- Mode: the most common value. Useful for categorical data.

For a symmetric distribution (like adult height), mean ≈ median ≈ mode. The 'typical' person is well-described by any of them.

For skewed distributions:
- Right-skewed (income, wealth, city size): mean > median > mode. A few huge values pull the mean up.
- Left-skewed (test scores with a ceiling): mean < median.

US household income (2022): mean ~115,000 USD, median ~75,000. The 'average household' as measured by mean is income that 60% of households fall below.

Dangers of using mean carelessly: 'the average net worth in this room is 100 million USD' (because Elon Musk just walked in). For policy and individual planning, median is often more informative.

The terms have legal force: a statement that 'most people earn the average wage' is misleading for income, even if it would be roughly true for height.
items.why: 'Average' has many meanings, and in skewed distributions they diverge dramatically. Almost every report on income, wealth or wait times that uses the word 'average' should be parsed carefully.
